newsitem.title: DUBAI: Forwarders/shippers clash at air cargo forum.
newsitem.headline: Forwarders/shippers clash at air cargo forum.

text.p: Old rivalries between air freight forwarders and their shipping customers and between airlines and shippers came into the open on Wednesday at the final day of the 18th Air Cargo Forum meeting.

Forwarders representatives made clear that they feel their role in the air cargo industry is continually pressured by demands from shippers -- invited to the forum for the first time in 36 years -- seeking a better quality of service and lower prices. They also fear shippers are starting to bypass them and deal direct with airlines in their ongoing efforts to reduce costs in logistics and transportation systems.

Industry speakers during the four day conference said the global air cargo industry generated annual revenues estimated between US$42 billion and US$50 billion. However the head of the U.S. based MergeGlobal consultancy said it "generated an estimated US$64 billion in retail revenue and 19.6 million tonnes of traffic in 1995."

Forwarders were responding to speeches earlier Wednesday by officials from the European Air Shippers Council (EASC) and the U.S. National Industrial Transportation League (NITL), inspired by an EASC report based on consultations across Europe, which set out what the shippers considered to be hurdles facing the modernisatiuon of the industry.

The president of the Swiss-based Panalpina forwarding group, Gerhard Fischer said, "there are major discrepanciess between shippers, forwarders and carriers ... we should try to convince shippers that we are a highly skilled and transparent industry."
"We want to be masters of the (traffic) flow" said Fischer adding that "airlines very often trespass in a field that should be reserved for forwarders."
He was backed by Air Express International (AEI) president Guenter Rohrmann who said, "the industry has never been more transparent".

EASC secretary general, Chris Welsh said its aims had been to break down barriers within the whole air cargo industry. But in reply to a question at a news conference said the situation was, "rather cloudy and opaque."

NITL's policy director, Peter Gatti said "forwarders are very nervous and they want to keep shippers completely away from airlines. They want to control the business but if they do not talk to customers, they will not be able to deliver the right product."
Gatti and Welsh told the news conference that talks betweeen airlines, forwarders and shippers would not raise any anti-trust problems in either the U.S. or the Eu.

Conference chairman and head of Air Foyle, Chris Foyle said in his closing remarks, "it is clear from this conference that shippers and the industry must get together more often. I am amazed by the defenciveness of the industry (forwarders) to the shippers who want improving quality and reduced prices. Afterall that's business."

Gatti said "the shipper is becoming more sophisticated and maybe the intergrators (such as Fedex or DHL are becoming a more attractive alternative by providing a customised service on a door to door basis." - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542-7706 Fax+44 171 542-5017
